questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls by using Azure Policy, including built-in and custom policy definitions
questions.prompt: You assign a policy with the Deny effect requiring HTTPS-only on storage accounts, at subscription scope. A week later compliance still reports 40% and no deployments have failed. What explains both observations, and what would change the number?
options: The assignment has no managed identity; add one and re-evaluate
Deny acts only on create and update requests; assign Modify or DeployIfNotExists and run a remediation task
The policy is in report-only mode; switch it to enforced
Compliance data refreshes monthly; wait for the next cycle
questions.explanation: Deny blocks new and changed resources and never touches existing ones, so pre-existing non-compliant accounts stay non-compliant and nothing fails because nobody deployed a new one. Remediating existing resources needs Modify or DeployIfNotExists plus a remediation task. Azure Policy has no report-only mode - that is Conditional Access.
why_not: A managed identity is needed by Modify and DeployIfNotExists to remediate, not by Deny. Adding one changes nothing about resources that already exist.
Azure Policy has no report-only mode. Report-only is a Conditional Access policy state.
Waiting changes nothing. Deny never acts on resources that already exist, so they stay non-compliant however often compliance is evaluated.

questions.prompt: A ReadOnly lock is applied to a storage account as a hardening measure. An application that only reads blobs stops working. Why?
options: ReadOnly locks block data-plane reads as well as writes
Listing storage account keys is a POST operation, which ReadOnly blocks
ReadOnly locks remove the application's role assignment
ReadOnly locks require the application to re-authenticate every hour
questions.explanation: Locks are control-plane controls. ReadOnly does not stop blob reads, but it does block operations implemented as POST that look like reads - listing account keys being the standard example. This is why CanNotDelete is the usual recommendation and ReadOnly causes more outages than it prevents.
why_not: Locks are control-plane controls. Blob reads are data plane and are not affected by a ReadOnly lock.
Locks do not remove or change role assignments.
Locks have nothing to do with authentication or token lifetime.

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure role-based access control (RBAC)
questions.prompt: A colleague's notes say to evaluate overprivileged assignments in the Microsoft Entra Permissions Management blade. What is wrong, and where would you do this now?
options: Nothing is wrong; the blade moved to the Defender portal
Permissions Management was retired; use CIEM capabilities in Defender CSPM, PIM access reviews, and Azure RBAC enumeration
Nothing is wrong, but it requires an add-on licence
Permissions Management was renamed Entra ID Governance; use that blade
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra Permissions Management was retired on 1 October 2025, with support ending 1 November 2025. Its entitlement capabilities live on inside Defender CSPM. This is one of the sharper traps in AZ-500-era material, and the SC-500 bullet is worded 'by using Azure role-based access control' for that reason.
why_not: Something is wrong: Permissions Management was retired on 1 October 2025, not moved.
No licence brings it back. The product was retired, and support ended on 1 November 2025.
It was not renamed. It was retired, and its entitlement capabilities live on in Defender CSPM.

questions.sub_skill: Configure security controls for backup protection by using Azure Backup security features
questions.prompt: Multi-user authorization is configured on a Recovery Services vault, with the Resource Guard in the same subscription and owned by the same administrator. What does this configuration protect against?
options: A compromised administrator account deleting backups
Accidental deletion by that administrator, but not a deliberate one
Nothing at all; MUA requires a separate tenant to function
Ransomware encrypting the recovery points
questions.explanation: MUA works only if the Resource Guard lives where the vault's administrator cannot reach it - a different subscription, ideally a different tenant, under different people. Same-owner MUA is a speed bump against accident and no defence against an attacker who already holds that account.
why_not: A compromised administrator who also owns the Resource Guard can approve their own critical operation.
MUA does function with the Resource Guard in the same subscription. It simply guards only against accident when one person controls both sides.
MUA adds a second approval to critical operations on the vault. It is not a control against data being encrypted.

questions.sub_skill: Manage custom roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
questions.prompt: A custom Azure role grants DataActions Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/secrets/* with NotDataActions Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/secrets/getSecret/action, so that a support team can manage secrets without reading their values. It is assigned to Priya on a key vault. Priya still retrieves a secret's value from that vault. Which two statements could each explain this?
options: Priya holds another role assignment, on the vault or at a scope above it, that includes getSecret/action - NotDataActions subtracts only within its own role and is not a deny
The vault uses the access policy permission model, where Azure RBAC data actions do not apply, and an access policy grants Priya secret permissions
The exclusion should have been Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/secrets/read under NotActions, which is what controls reading a secret's value
Priya also holds Key Vault Reader on the vault, which includes reading secret values
questions.explanation: Effective access is the union of every role assignment at the scope and above. NotDataActions removes a data action from its own role only - Microsoft's documentation states it is not a deny rule - so a second assignment that includes getSecret/action still grants it. Separately, Azure RBAC data actions govern only vaults on the Azure RBAC permission model; on an access policy vault, the policy decides, so check enableRbacAuthorization before debugging anything else. Only a deny assignment, which you cannot create directly, overrides a grant.
why_not: Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/secrets/read is a control-plane action that views a secret's properties, not its value. Reading the value is the data action getSecret/action, so NotDataActions is the right place for this exclusion.
Key Vault Reader reads metadata only. It cannot read secret contents.
questions.concept: NotDataActions is not a deny; the vault's permission model decides
questions.misconception: An exclusion in one role definition blocks the permission everywhere

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate regulatory compliance by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.prompt: An auditor asks which PCI DSS controls your Azure subscription currently fails, and which of your resources are responsible. Defender for Cloud is enabled on the subscription. Where do you get this answer?
options: The secure score, filtered to the recommendations with the highest score impact
The PCI DSS audit report for Azure in the Microsoft Service Trust Portal
The Regulatory compliance dashboard, after adding the PCI DSS standard to the subscription
The Microsoft cloud security benchmark, which is applied by default and covers PCI DSS on its own
questions.explanation: Additional standards are assigned to a subscription or management group and then appear in the Regulatory compliance dashboard, which maps each control in the framework to the recommendations - and so the resources - that evidence it.
why_not: Secure score is computed from the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. It helps you prioritise recommendations; it does not map them to PCI DSS controls.
The Service Trust Portal documents Microsoft's own compliance as the cloud provider. It says nothing about how your resources are configured.
The Microsoft cloud security benchmark is the default standard and the basis of secure score. PCI DSS still has to be added as a standard of its own before its controls appear in the dashboard.
questions.misconception: Secure score or the provider's audit reports show your own framework compliance

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls in Defender for Cloud, including security standards and recommendations
questions.prompt: A Defender for Cloud recommendation flags a storage account used only by an isolated test harness. The risk has been formally accepted until the harness is decommissioned in three months. The account must stay visible in compliance reporting with the reason recorded, and the waiver must end on its own. What should you do?
options: Disable the recommendation in the Microsoft cloud security benchmark for the subscription
Create an exemption for that resource on the recommendation, with a justification and an expiration date
Move the storage account to a resource group excluded from the standard's assignment scope
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to the storage account and record the accepted risk in the lock's notes
questions.explanation: An exemption keeps the resource in scope but records a justified waiver, which flows into the compliance view instead of disappearing from it, and an expiration date ends the waiver without anyone having to remember to remove it.
why_not: Disabling the recommendation removes it for every resource in the subscription, not just this one, and records no per-resource reason.
An exclusion takes the scope out of the assignment entirely, so the account is no longer evaluated and no longer appears in compliance reporting.
A lock controls deletion on the management plane. It has no effect on recommendations or on compliance reporting.
questions.misconception: Removing a resource from scope is the same as accepting its risk

questions.prompt: Alex holds the Owner role at a management group. To make Alex read-only in subscription Sub1, which sits under that management group, an administrator assigns Alex the Reader role at Sub1. What is Alex's effective access in Sub1, and what would actually make it read-only?
options: Reader - the more specific scope takes precedence, so nothing further is needed
Owner - assignments are additive and inherited, so the Owner assignment at the management group must be replaced by assignments at only the scopes Alex should administer
Owner - add a condition to the Reader assignment that denies write operations
Owner - create a deny assignment for write operations on Sub1 from the Access control (IAM) blade
questions.explanation: Effective permission is the union of every assignment at the scope and above it. There is no ordering and no precedence by specificity, so the inherited Owner assignment still applies in Sub1. The fix is to stop granting Owner at the parent scope.
why_not: Azure RBAC has no precedence by scope. A Reader assignment adds nothing to, and removes nothing from, an Owner assignment inherited from above.
A condition narrows only what its own assignment grants. It cannot take away permissions granted by a different assignment.
You cannot create deny assignments directly; they are created by platform features such as Azure managed applications.
questions.misconception: A more specific role assignment overrides an inherited one

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls by using infrastructure as code
questions.prompt: Developers deploy storage accounts with Bicep through Azure Pipelines from an Azure Repos repository. Requirements: a storage account that allows anonymous blob access must never be created, whichever tool deploys it; and developers must see IaC misconfigurations as comments on the pull request before it is merged. Which two actions meet the requirements? Each correct answer is part of the solution.
options: Assign an Azure Policy definition with the Deny effect that blocks storage accounts allowing anonymous blob access
Assign the same policy definition with the Audit effect and review the compliance results weekly
Connect the Azure DevOps organisation to Defender for Cloud DevOps security, run the Microsoft Security DevOps extension in the pipeline, and enable pull request annotations
Enable Defender for Storage on the subscription
questions.explanation: A Bicep deployment is a series of Azure Resource Manager requests, so a Deny policy blocks a non-compliant template exactly as it blocks a portal click - the platform enforces it, whoever deploys. Catching the problem before merge is DevOps security: Microsoft Security DevOps runs IaC analysers in the pipeline, and with pull request annotations enabled the findings appear on the pull request.
why_not: Audit reports non-compliance after the resource already exists. The requirement is that it is never created.
Defender for Storage detects threats against storage at runtime. It neither blocks configurations nor comments on pull requests.
questions.concept: Policy guardrails plus pre-deployment IaC scanning
questions.misconception: An Audit policy prevents non-compliant deployments
